1 # Tutorial: Compose integrations into a system 2 3 In this tutorial you compose two integrations into a **system**: a named composition of integrations that are developed and tested independently but run and observed together. You scaffold an extractor that publishes order messages and a loader that consumes them, verify each one alone, then declare their topology in a **SystemHost** and run the whole flow with one command. 4 5 The [transactional tutorial](../transactional/index.md) teaches what happens *inside* an integration; this one is about what happens *between* them. Both scaffolds ship with working sample logic, so you won't implement a single pipeline step here — the chapters spend their time on composition. 6 7 ## Before you begin 8 9 - You've completed the [transactional tutorial](../transactional/index.md) — this series assumes its tools and vocabulary and doesn't re-teach pipeline authoring 10 - Tools installed: .NET SDK 10, Docker Desktop (running — the system provisions a Redis container), Dapr CLI 1.16+ initialized (`dapr init`), [Task](https://taskfile.dev) 11 - The [Intropy CLI installed](../../get-started/install.md) and on your `PATH` 12 - No separate .NET Aspire install: the SystemHost is an ordinary .NET project, and the orchestration and dashboard arrive as NuGet packages on first restore 13 - A scratch directory you don't mind throwing away 14 15 ## What you'll build 16 17 The `order-flow` system: an `order-extractor` integration that sweeps order files from an inbound folder and publishes each one as a message, and an `order-loader` integration that subscribes and writes each order to a destination folder. The message's shape lives in neither of them: the first scaffold also creates a shared `Contracts` project, and both integrations compile against its `Order` record. 18 19 ```mermaid 20 flowchart LR 21 src[(Inbound folder
orders/*.json)]:::ext 22 subgraph sys [system: order-flow] 23 direction LR 24 E[order-extractor
sweep → publish]:::block 25 T{{pub/sub pubsub
topic orders}}:::topic 26 L[order-loader
subscribe → load]:::block 27 E --> T --> L 28 end 29 dst[(Destination folder)]:::ext 30 src --> E 31 L --> dst 32 33 classDef block fill:#1e1a2e,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#e6e1f5; 34 classDef topic fill:#0f0d1a,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1px,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#e6e1f5; 35 classDef ext fill:#0f0d1a,stroke:#21EAC7,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#cfeee6; 36 style sys fill:#141225,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1px,color:#c8bfe8; 37 ``` 38 39 The pub/sub in the middle is the interesting part. When an integration runs on its own, that component is private and in-memory: the extractor publishes into a void, and the loader only sees messages you inject by hand. Run through the SystemHost, both sidecars load a system-scoped pub/sub instead — generated from the topology and backed by Redis — and the extractor's messages reach the loader. Same code, same component names, different backing. That resolution rule is the heart of the tutorial. 40 41 The SystemHost itself is a .NET Aspire AppHost holding the system's source of truth: one class declares the integrations and the typed topic refs that connect them, validated before anything runs. Run it and it starts every integration with its Dapr sidecar, generates and provisions the system-scoped components, and serves a dashboard with logs and traces for the whole system. The same declaration feeds a generation backend, so running locally and generating deployment artifacts are two views of one model. 42 43 ## The chapters 44 45 Each chapter introduces one thing, ends in a runnable command, and leaves you with working code. You can stop after any of them. 46 47 1. [The extractor](01-extractor.md) — scaffold `order-extractor` (and the shared `Contracts` library that comes with it) and run it alone on isolated components 48 2. [The loader](02-loader.md) — scaffold `order-loader` against the same shared contract and verify a subscriber in isolation through its own sidecar 49 3. [The SystemHost](03-systemhost.md) — scaffold the host and read the typed topology `sys create` assembled from your scaffolds, then validate it with `check` 50 4. [System-scoped components](04-component-scoping.md) — how sidecars resolve components: the local set standalone, the generated overlay under the host 51 5. [Run the system](05-run-the-system.md) — one command, both integrations, one distributed trace 52

# Tutorial: Compose integrations into a system In this tutorial you compose two integrations into a **system**: a named composition of integrations that are developed and tested independently but run and observed together. You scaffold an extractor that publishes order messages and a loader that consumes them, verify each one alone, then declare their topology in a **SystemHost** and run the whole flow with one command. The [transactional tutorial](../transactional/index.md) teaches what happens *inside* an integration; this one is about what happens *between* them. Both scaffolds ship with working sample logic, so you won't implement a single pipeline step here — the chapters spend their time on composition. ## Before you begin - You've completed the [transactional tutorial](../transactional/index.md) — this series assumes its tools and vocabulary and doesn't re-teach pipeline authoring - Tools installed: .NET SDK 10, Docker Desktop (running — the system provisions a Redis container), Dapr CLI 1.16+ initialized (`dapr init`), [Task](https://taskfile.dev) - The [Intropy CLI installed](../../get-started/install.md) and on your `PATH` - No separate .NET Aspire install: the SystemHost is an ordinary .NET project, and the orchestration and dashboard arrive as NuGet packages on first restore - A scratch directory you don't mind throwing away ## What you'll build The `order-flow` system: an `order-extractor` integration that sweeps order files from an inbound folder and publishes each one as a message, and an `order-loader` integration that subscribes and writes each order to a destination folder. The message's shape lives in neither of them: the first scaffold also creates a shared `Contracts` project, and both integrations compile against its `Order` record. ```mermaid flowchart LR src[(Inbound folder
orders/*.json)]:::ext subgraph sys [system: order-flow] direction LR E[order-extractor
sweep → publish]:::block T{{pub/sub pubsub
topic orders}}:::topic L[order-loader
subscribe → load]:::block E --> T --> L end dst[(Destination folder)]:::ext src --> E L --> dst classDef block fill:#1e1a2e,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#e6e1f5; classDef topic fill:#0f0d1a,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1px,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#e6e1f5; classDef ext fill:#0f0d1a,stroke:#21EAC7,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#cfeee6; style sys fill:#141225,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1px,color:#c8bfe8; ``` The pub/sub in the middle is the interesting part. When an integration runs on its own, that component is private and in-memory: the extractor publishes into a void, and the loader only sees messages you inject by hand. Run through the SystemHost, both sidecars load a system-scoped pub/sub instead — generated from the topology and backed by Redis — and the extractor's messages reach the loader. Same code, same component names, different backing. That resolution rule is the heart of the tutorial. The SystemHost itself is a .NET Aspire AppHost holding the system's source of truth: one class declares the integrations and the typed topic refs that connect them, validated before anything runs. Run it and it starts every integration with its Dapr sidecar, generates and provisions the system-scoped components, and serves a dashboard with logs and traces for the whole system. The same declaration feeds a generation backend, so running locally and generating deployment artifacts are two views of one model. ## The chapters Each chapter introduces one thing, ends in a runnable command, and leaves you with working code. You can stop after any of them. 1. [The extractor](01-extractor.md) — scaffold `order-extractor` (and the shared `Contracts` library that comes with it) and run it alone on isolated components 2. [The loader](02-loader.md) — scaffold `order-loader` against the same shared contract and verify a subscriber in isolation through its own sidecar 3. [The SystemHost](03-systemhost.md) — scaffold the host and read the typed topology `sys create` assembled from your scaffolds, then validate it with `check` 4. [System-scoped components](04-component-scoping.md) — how sidecars resolve components: the local set standalone, the generated overlay under the host 5. [Run the system](05-run-the-system.md) — one command, both integrations, one distributed trace

# 1. The extractor

In this chapter you create the system workspace, scaffold the first of its two integrations, and run it alone: a complete integration on its own isolated components, before any system exists.

## Scaffold

Create the workspace and render the `extractor` blueprint into it:

```bash
mkdir order-flow && cd order-flow
intropy int create extractor -n OrderExtractor -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-extractor
```

`order-flow/` is the system workspace: a plain directory that holds the two integrations and, from chapter 3, the SystemHost as siblings. Nothing about it is special. Each integration stays an independent project you could version, test, and deploy on its own.

Two flags deserve a closer look:

- **`-s topic=orders`:** the pub/sub topic the extractor publishes to. You'll type the same value when scaffolding the loader — each scaffold declares its own half of the contract, and records it (in `.intropy/scaffold.json`) for the system to assemble in chapter 3.
- **No `empty=true`:** unlike the transactional tutorial, you keep the blueprint's sample logic. This tutorial is about what happens between integrations, so the insides stay stock.

The render's last line reports a project you didn't ask for: `created dependency Contracts from template shared-contracts`. The workspace now holds two directories:

```
order-flow/
├── Contracts/                    # shared contract types — scaffolded once per workspace
│   ├── Contracts.csproj
│   ├── Order.cs                  # the order contract the extractor publishes
│   └── OrderLine.cs
└── order-extractor/
    ├── Taskfile.yml              # task run / build / test
    ├── docker-compose.yml        # local observability stack — standalone runs only
    ├── local/
    │   ├── dapr-components/
    │   │   ├── poll.yaml         # cron binding — sweeps the inbound folder every 5 s
    │   │   ├── inbound.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the source system
    │   │   └── pubsub.yaml       # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
    │   └── sample-data/
    │       └── sample-order.json
    ├── src/                      # implemented: sweep inbound, transform, publish
    └── test/
```

The extractor itself looks like the transactional layout you know, with its own components. `Contracts/` is new: the extractor template declares the `shared-contracts` template as a dependency, so scaffolding the first block into a workspace also scaffolds the workspace's contract library next to it. It holds the `Order` record (and its `OrderLine` lines): the shape the extractor publishes, defined in neither block because both halves of the system need it. The extractor references it as an ordinary `ProjectReference` (`../../Contracts/Contracts.csproj`); its own source shape stays private in `src/Model/In.cs`, and the pipeline's transform step maps that `In` to the shared `Order` before publishing.

The sample logic ships working. On every poll tick it lists the inbound folder, publishes each file's content as an `Order` message on topic `orders`, and deletes the source file. And unlike the transactional integration, which runs once and exits, the extractor keeps running until you stop it — that matters in chapter 5, when you'll drop files in while the whole system is live.

## Check it

Run the extractor standalone:

```bash
cd order-extractor
task run
```

The task seeds `sample-order.json` into the inbound folder and starts the integration under Dapr, with the sidecar loading only `local/dapr-components/`. Within a poll tick you should see:

```
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Swept 1 file from inbound
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)
```

Stop it with Ctrl+C, then confirm the source file is gone:

```bash
ls local/storage/inbound/
```

The folder is empty: the extractor swept the file, published it, and cleaned up.

Where did the message go? Into the extractor's own in-memory pub/sub — and nothing subscribes there. That's the point of an isolated run: it verifies the extractor's whole job (sweep, publish, clean up) without needing a consumer to exist. Delivery to a consumer is the system's job, and that's chapter 5.

!!! check "Recap"
    - Created the `order-flow` workspace; integrations and the SystemHost live in it as siblings
    - Scaffolded `order-extractor` from the `extractor` blueprint with its sample logic intact
    - The render also scaffolded `Contracts/`, the workspace's shared contract library — the `Order` record the extractor publishes lives there, not in the extractor
    - Standalone, the sidecar loads only `local/dapr-components/`: an isolated, in-memory world
    - The published message intentionally went nowhere — no consumer exists yet

1	# 2. The loader
2	
3	In this chapter you scaffold `order-loader`, the consuming half of the system, and verify it the way any subscriber is verified in isolation: by publishing through its own sidecar.
4	
5	## Scaffold
6	
7	From the workspace root, render the `loader` blueprint:
8	
9	```bash
10	intropy int create loader -n OrderLoader -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-loader
11	```
12	
13	`-s topic=orders` is the same value you gave the extractor, and typing it twice is deliberate: each integration declares its own half of the contract and stays verifiable alone. Chapter 3 assembles the two halves into one typed declaration — and checks that they meet.
14	
15	The message *shape*, though, is not typed twice. The loader template declares the same `shared-contracts` dependency as the extractor, and this time the render finds the project already in place:
16	
17	```
18	dependency Contracts already scaffolded from shared-contracts — skipped
19	```
20	
21	The first block into a workspace creates `Contracts/`; every later one detects it by its scaffold record and reuses it. Both blocks now compile against the same `Order` record, so the shape of the messages crossing the system has exactly one definition.
22	
23	```
24	order-loader/
25	├── Taskfile.yml
26	├── docker-compose.yml
27	├── local/
28	│   └── dapr-components/
29	│       ├── pubsub.yaml           # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
30	│       └── destination.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the destination system
31	├── src/                          # implemented: subscribe to topic, deserialize, validate, load
32	└── test/
33	```
34	
35	The sample logic subscribes to `orders` on `pubsub` and, for each message, deserializes it into the shared `Order` record, validates it, and writes `{orderId}.json` through the `destination` binding. The mirror image of the extractor's shape handling: the loader consumes the shared `Order` and maps it to its own private destination shape in `src/Model/Out.cs`. Like the extractor, it runs until you stop it.
36	
37	Note that `pubsub.yaml` here has the same component name as the extractor's — but they are not the same broker. Each in-memory pub/sub lives inside its own integration's sidecar, so two standalone runs are two separate worlds. Keep that in mind; chapter 4 turns it into the mechanism the whole system rests on.
38	
39	## Publish through the loader's own sidecar
40	
41	A subscriber alone has a problem the extractor didn't: nothing publishes to it. The answer follows from where the broker lives. The in-memory pub/sub exists *inside the loader's sidecar*, so any publish routed through that sidecar reaches the subscription — and `dapr publish --publish-app-id` does exactly that.
42	
43	Start the loader in one terminal:
44	
45	```bash
46	cd order-loader
47	task run
48	```
49	
50	Wait for the subscription to register:
51	
52	```
53	== APP == info: OrderLoader.Pipeline[0]
54	== APP ==       Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)
55	```
56	
57	## Check it
58	
59	In a second terminal, publish an order through the loader's sidecar:
60	
61	```bash
62	dapr publish --publish-app-id order-loader --pubsub pubsub --topic orders \
63	  --data '{"orderId":"ORD-2001","customerId":"CUST-42","orderDate":"2026-07-24T09:30:00Z","lines":[{"sku":"SKU-AAA","quantity":1,"unitPrice":12.50}]}'
64	```
65	
66	```
67	Event published successfully
68	```
69	
70	The loader picks it up and writes the destination file:
71	
72	```bash
73	cat local/storage/destination/ORD-2001.json
74	```
75	
76	```json
77	{"OrderId":"ORD-2001","CustomerId":"CUST-42","LoadedAt":"2026-07-24T09:31:12Z","Status":"Loaded"}
78	```
79	
80	Stop the loader with Ctrl+C.
81	
82	!!! check "Recap"
83	    - Scaffolded `order-loader`: subscribes to `orders` on `pubsub`, writes each order through the `destination` binding
84	    - The loader's render found `Contracts/` already scaffolded and skipped it — both blocks compile against one shared `Order` record
85	    - A subscriber is verified in isolation by publishing through its own sidecar — that's where its in-memory broker lives
86	    - Both integrations now work alone, each in its own isolated world; nothing connects them yet

# 2. The loader

In this chapter you scaffold `order-loader`, the consuming half of the system, and verify it the way any subscriber is verified in isolation: by publishing through its own sidecar.

## Scaffold

From the workspace root, render the `loader` blueprint:

```bash
intropy int create loader -n OrderLoader -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-loader
```

`-s topic=orders` is the same value you gave the extractor, and typing it twice is deliberate: each integration declares its own half of the contract and stays verifiable alone. Chapter 3 assembles the two halves into one typed declaration — and checks that they meet.

The message *shape*, though, is not typed twice. The loader template declares the same `shared-contracts` dependency as the extractor, and this time the render finds the project already in place:

```
dependency Contracts already scaffolded from shared-contracts — skipped
```

The first block into a workspace creates `Contracts/`; every later one detects it by its scaffold record and reuses it. Both blocks now compile against the same `Order` record, so the shape of the messages crossing the system has exactly one definition.

```
order-loader/
├── Taskfile.yml
├── docker-compose.yml
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/
│       ├── pubsub.yaml           # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
│       └── destination.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the destination system
├── src/                          # implemented: subscribe to topic, deserialize, validate, load
└── test/
```

The sample logic subscribes to `orders` on `pubsub` and, for each message, deserializes it into the shared `Order` record, validates it, and writes `{orderId}.json` through the `destination` binding. The mirror image of the extractor's shape handling: the loader consumes the shared `Order` and maps it to its own private destination shape in `src/Model/Out.cs`. Like the extractor, it runs until you stop it.

Note that `pubsub.yaml` here has the same component name as the extractor's — but they are not the same broker. Each in-memory pub/sub lives inside its own integration's sidecar, so two standalone runs are two separate worlds. Keep that in mind; chapter 4 turns it into the mechanism the whole system rests on.

## Publish through the loader's own sidecar

A subscriber alone has a problem the extractor didn't: nothing publishes to it. The answer follows from where the broker lives. The in-memory pub/sub exists *inside the loader's sidecar*, so any publish routed through that sidecar reaches the subscription — and `dapr publish --publish-app-id` does exactly that.

Start the loader in one terminal:

```bash
cd order-loader
task run
```

Wait for the subscription to register:

```
== APP == info: OrderLoader.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)
```

## Check it

In a second terminal, publish an order through the loader's sidecar:

```bash
dapr publish --publish-app-id order-loader --pubsub pubsub --topic orders \
  --data '{"orderId":"ORD-2001","customerId":"CUST-42","orderDate":"2026-07-24T09:30:00Z","lines":[{"sku":"SKU-AAA","quantity":1,"unitPrice":12.50}]}'
```

```
Event published successfully
```

The loader picks it up and writes the destination file:

```bash
cat local/storage/destination/ORD-2001.json
```

```json
{"OrderId":"ORD-2001","CustomerId":"CUST-42","LoadedAt":"2026-07-24T09:31:12Z","Status":"Loaded"}
```

Stop the loader with Ctrl+C.

!!! check "Recap"
    - Scaffolded `order-loader`: subscribes to `orders` on `pubsub`, writes each order through the `destination` binding
    - The loader's render found `Contracts/` already scaffolded and skipped it — both blocks compile against one shared `Order` record
    - A subscriber is verified in isolation by publishing through its own sidecar — that's where its in-memory broker lives
    - Both integrations now work alone, each in its own isolated world; nothing connects them yet

1	# 3. The SystemHost
2	
3	In this chapter you scaffold the SystemHost and read the file it exists for: the system's topology,
4	declared as typed C# and validated before anything runs.
5	
6	A SystemHost is a .NET Aspire AppHost with one Intropy-specific job: it holds the system's source
7	of truth. One class declares which integrations exist and which topics connect them; everything
8	else the host does — running the system locally, generating its Dapr components, validating the
9	composition — is a backend over that one declaration. There is nothing to install; the
10	orchestration, the dashboard, and the topology model arrive as NuGet packages on first restore.
11	
12	## Scaffold
13	
14	From the workspace root:
15	
16	```bash
17	intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host
18	```
19	
20	The noun is `sys`, not `int`, because a SystemHost is not an integration: it has no pipeline, no
21	app id, no blueprint parameters. The name derivation is the one you already know: `OrderFlow`
22	kebab-cases to `order-flow`, the system's name.
23	
24	The command reads before it writes. Each scaffold in chapters 1 and 2 left a record of what it
25	declared — its blueprint kind and the topic you passed with `-s topic=orders`, in
26	`.intropy/scaffold.json` — and `sys create` scans the workspace for those records and assembles
27	them into a typed declaration. `Contracts/` has a record too, marked as a shared library rather than
28	a block, so the host reads it as the contract project: referenced, never declared as a component.
29	
30	```
31	system-host/
32	├── OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj   # .NET Aspire AppHost project
33	├── Program.cs                    # one entry point, two backends — you don't edit this file
34	├── OrderFlowSystem.cs            # the system definition, assembled from the scaffold records
35	├── Topics.cs                     # the system's topics, as typed refs
36	├── Properties/
37	│   └── launchSettings.json       # dashboard and OTLP ports
38	└── Taskfile.yml                  # task run → dotnet run
39	```
40	
41	One thing is conspicuously absent: a `dapr-components/` directory. The system's components are not
42	files anyone maintains — they are generated from the declaration you are about to read. Chapter 4
43	watches that happen.
44	
45	## One entry point, two backends
46	
47	```csharp title="system-host/Program.cs"
48	using System.Reflection;
49	using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;
50	using Intropy.Topology.Generation;
51	
52	var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
53	
54	return args is ["run", ..] or []
55	    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)      // dotnet run → the system, live (chapter 5)
56	    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);   // check | graph | generate → the model, inspected
57	```
58	
59	Both branches start the same way: discover the one system definition in this assembly, build it,
60	validate it. Only then do they diverge — into a live run under the Aspire dashboard, or into
61	verbs that inspect and export the model without starting anything. F5 and a deployment manifest
62	are two backends of the same truth, which is why the declaration can afford to be the only place
63	that truth lives.
64	
65	## The declaration
66	
67	Open `Topics.cs`. The topic you typed into two scaffolds is now a single value:
68	
69	```csharp title="system-host/Topics.cs"
70	using Intropy.Topology;
71	using Contracts;
72	
73	/// <summary>The system's topics, each defined once and shared by every component that touches it.</summary>
74	public static class Topics
75	{
76	    /// <summary>Order messages flowing from the extractor to the loader.</summary>
77	    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
78	}
79	```
80	
81	`OrderFlowSystem.cs` is the topology itself:
82	
83	```csharp title="system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs"
84	using Intropy.Topology;
85	
86	/// <summary>The order-flow system: what exists, and what connects it.</summary>
87	public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
88	{
89	    public string SystemName => "order-flow";
90	
91	    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
92	    {
93	        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
94	        builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);
95	    }
96	}
97	```
98	
99	Nothing in these files is new information. `AddExtractor` and `AddLoader` name the blueprints you
100	scaffolded; `"pubsub"` and `"orders"` are the component and topic names from chapters 1 and 2.
101	What `sys create` did is assemble your scaffold-time declarations into one place and give them a
102	type. From here on, this is where the topology lives: adding an integration or renaming a topic
103	means editing this declaration, and the rest of the chapter is about why that is safe.
104	
105	Three things about the shape:
106	
107	- **A topic is a value, not a string typed twice:** `Topics.Orders` is defined once — pubsub
108	  component name, topic name, and the contract type its messages carry — and referenced by both
109	  components. There is no second copy to drift.
110	- **The edge is derived:** no call says "the loader depends on the extractor". Both components
111	  touching `Topics.Orders` *is* the wiring; the dashboard edge and the startup ordering you'll see
112	  in chapter 5 fall out of it.
113	- **Block kinds surface at the host:** the declaration rhymes with the scaffolds. An extractor can
114	  `Publishes` but has nothing to subscribe with; a loader is the reverse. Declaring an edge a Block
115	  cannot have is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
116	
117	And one thing about what is *not* declared: a pub/sub registration. `Topics.Orders` names its

# 3. The SystemHost

In this chapter you scaffold the SystemHost and read the file it exists for: the system's topology,
declared as typed C# and validated before anything runs.

A SystemHost is a .NET Aspire AppHost with one Intropy-specific job: it holds the system's source
of truth. One class declares which integrations exist and which topics connect them; everything
else the host does — running the system locally, generating its Dapr components, validating the
composition — is a backend over that one declaration. There is nothing to install; the
orchestration, the dashboard, and the topology model arrive as NuGet packages on first restore.

## Scaffold

From the workspace root:

```bash
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host
```

The noun is `sys`, not `int`, because a SystemHost is not an integration: it has no pipeline, no
app id, no blueprint parameters. The name derivation is the one you already know: `OrderFlow`
kebab-cases to `order-flow`, the system's name.

The command reads before it writes. Each scaffold in chapters 1 and 2 left a record of what it
declared — its blueprint kind and the topic you passed with `-s topic=orders`, in
`.intropy/scaffold.json` — and `sys create` scans the workspace for those records and assembles
them into a typed declaration. `Contracts/` has a record too, marked as a shared library rather than
a block, so the host reads it as the contract project: referenced, never declared as a component.

```
system-host/
├── OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj   # .NET Aspire AppHost project
├── Program.cs                    # one entry point, two backends — you don't edit this file
├── OrderFlowSystem.cs            # the system definition, assembled from the scaffold records
├── Topics.cs                     # the system's topics, as typed refs
├── Properties/
│   └── launchSettings.json       # dashboard and OTLP ports
└── Taskfile.yml                  # task run → dotnet run
```

One thing is conspicuously absent: a `dapr-components/` directory. The system's components are not
files anyone maintains — they are generated from the declaration you are about to read. Chapter 4
watches that happen.

## One entry point, two backends

```csharp title="system-host/Program.cs"
using System.Reflection;
using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;

var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();

return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)      // dotnet run → the system, live (chapter 5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);   // check | graph | generate → the model, inspected
```

Both branches start the same way: discover the one system definition in this assembly, build it,
validate it. Only then do they diverge — into a live run under the Aspire dashboard, or into
verbs that inspect and export the model without starting anything. F5 and a deployment manifest
are two backends of the same truth, which is why the declaration can afford to be the only place
that truth lives.

## The declaration

Open `Topics.cs`. The topic you typed into two scaffolds is now a single value:

```csharp title="system-host/Topics.cs"
using Intropy.Topology;
using Contracts;

/// <summary>The system's topics, each defined once and shared by every component that touches it.</summary>
public static class Topics
{
    /// <summary>Order messages flowing from the extractor to the loader.</summary>
    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
}
```

`OrderFlowSystem.cs` is the topology itself:

```csharp title="system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs"
using Intropy.Topology;

/// <summary>The order-flow system: what exists, and what connects it.</summary>
public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-flow";

    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
        builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);
    }
}
```

Nothing in these files is new information. `AddExtractor` and `AddLoader` name the blueprints you
scaffolded; `"pubsub"` and `"orders"` are the component and topic names from chapters 1 and 2.
What `sys create` did is assemble your scaffold-time declarations into one place and give them a
type. From here on, this is where the topology lives: adding an integration or renaming a topic
means editing this declaration, and the rest of the chapter is about why that is safe.

Three things about the shape:

- **A topic is a value, not a string typed twice:** `Topics.Orders` is defined once — pubsub
  component name, topic name, and the contract type its messages carry — and referenced by both
  components. There is no second copy to drift.
- **The edge is derived:** no call says "the loader depends on the extractor". Both components
  touching `Topics.Orders` *is* the wiring; the dashboard edge and the startup ordering you'll see
  in chapter 5 fall out of it.
- **Block kinds surface at the host:** the declaration rhymes with the scaffolds. An extractor can
  `Publishes` but has nothing to subscribe with; a loader is the reverse. Declaring an edge a Block
  cannot have is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.

And one thing about what is *not* declared: a pub/sub registration. `Topics.Orders` names its
pubsub component, so the system already knows it needs one — Redis gets provisioned in chapter 5
because a topic exists, not because anyone asked for a broker.

`Order`, the type parameter, is the contract the topic carries: the same record from the
workspace's `Contracts/` library that the extractor's transform step produces and the loader's
deserializer consumes. `sys create` recognized the library by its scaffold record and referenced
it from the host instead of generating a contract of its own, so the declaration doesn't just say
that both ends touch a topic named `orders` — it carries the very type both compile against. The
wiring itself only uses the names; the type documents the contract at the declaration site and
gives schema-aware tooling something to reflect on.

## Declared, then enforced

A declaration you edit by hand needs a gate, and `Build()` is it: whenever the host starts, and
whenever you run `check`, the declaration is validated as a whole. Any breach fails before a
single process starts.

Try it. Point the loader at a topic nobody publishes — the kind of mistake that used to live until
runtime:

```csharp title="system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs" hl_lines="2"
builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "oders"));
```

```bash
dotnet run -- check
```

```
error: The system topology is invalid (2 error(s)):
  ITP208 [Error] topic 'orders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is published but no component subscribes to it.
  ITP209 [Error] topic 'oders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is subscribed to but no component publishes it.
```

Both halves of the broken contract surface at once: the real topic is orphaned, and the misspelled
one has no producer. Undo the edit before moving on — the loader subscribes to `Topics.Orders`.

## How the declaration reaches the code

The host never rewrites your integrations. At run time, each integration binds its topic and
component names from runtime configuration: standalone, the scaffold's local files supply it;
under the SystemHost, the host generates it from this declaration and injects it. It is the same
swap you'll watch happen to the Dapr components in chapter 4 — the code is identical in both
modes, and only who supplies the configuration changes.

!!! info
    The declaration flow is the contract: scaffolds record what they declared, `sys create`
    assembles the records, and from then on the host's declaration is authoritative. Parts of the
    runtime half are still landing in the tooling — verify the generated-config binding against
    the shipped SystemHost packages before relying on it.

## Check it

```bash
cd system-host
dotnet run -- check
```

```
ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components).
```

`check` builds and validates the topology without starting anything. Its sibling prints the model
itself:

```bash
dotnet run -- graph
```

```json
{
  "systemName": "order-flow",
  "components": [
    { "name": "order-extractor", "kind": "extractor", "publishes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] },
    { "name": "order-loader", "kind": "loader", "subscribes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] }
  ],
  "topics": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "name": "orders", "contract": "Order" }]
}
```

That JSON is the system: the same model the run backend translates into containers and sidecars in
chapter 5, and the generate backend turns into deployable artifacts. Two backends, one truth.

!!! check "Recap"
    - `sys create` assembled the scaffolds' records into a typed declaration: `Topics.cs` defines
      each topic once, typed with the shared `Order` record from `Contracts/`, and
      `OrderFlowSystem.cs` wires components to it
    - The extractor→loader edge is derived from sharing `Topics.Orders`; block kinds at the host
      mirror the blueprints
    - `Build()` validates the whole declaration; `dotnet run -- check` runs the same gate from the
      command line
    - `dotnet run -- graph` prints the model both backends consume; nothing has run yet

# 4. System-scoped components

In this chapter you learn how the same integration code loads different Dapr components depending on who starts it: its own local set when run standalone, the system's generated overlay under the SystemHost.

## One file you wrote, one the host generates

Open the extractor's pub/sub component:

```yaml title="order-extractor/local/dapr-components/pubsub.yaml"
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: pubsub
spec:
  type: pubsub.in-memory
  version: v1
```

The system's counterpart is not a file you wrote. There is no `dapr-components/` directory in `system-host/`, and chapter 3's declaration never mentioned Redis. The host derives it: `Topics.Orders` names a pubsub component called `pubsub`, so the run backend generates one, backed by Redis because that is what the local run profile provisions:

```yaml title="system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml (generated)"
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: pubsub
spec:
  type: pubsub.redis
  version: v1
  metadata:
    - name: redisHost
      value: localhost:6379
```

Same `metadata.name`, different `spec.type`. That shared name is the whole mechanism: application code addresses components by name and never learns which backing is behind it. Whoever starts the sidecar decides which file the name resolves to — and on the system side that file is generated from the topology, so the model you validated in chapter 3 and the YAML the sidecar loads cannot disagree.

## The overlay

Standalone, you've already seen the answer: `task run` starts the sidecar with `--resources-path ./local/dapr-components`, so the integration gets its isolated, in-memory world.

Under the SystemHost, the host stages an *effective component set* for each integration before starting its sidecar:

1. Generate the system's components from the topology: one Redis-backed `pubsub`, because `Topics.Orders` names it.
2. Copy everything from the integration's `local/dapr-components/`.
3. Overlay the generated components: a generated component with the same `metadata.name` replaces the local one; new names are added.
4. Start the sidecar with `--resources-path` pointing at the staged directory, under `system-host/obj/dapr-components/<integration-name>/`.

For the extractor that means `poll.yaml` and `inbound.yaml` pass through untouched — sweeping a local folder is the integration's own business in both modes — while the local `pubsub.yaml` is replaced by the generated one.

Why an overlay, rather than handing the sidecar both directories? Because Dapr refuses duplicate component names across resource paths, and the duplicate name *is* the mechanism. And why not have the host generate a complete set? Then the topology would have to describe every folder binding in every integration — concerns that are the integration's own business, not the system's.

The overlay has edges worth knowing: it is staged when the host starts, so changing the topology means restarting the SystemHost; it keys on `metadata.name`, not the filename; and a generated component applies to every integration in the system. The Redis port is pinned to 6379, so the YAML above is exactly what the sidecars load. The staged files are real YAML on disk — inspect them whenever resolution surprises you — but editing them is futile: they are regenerated from the model on every start. Change the declaration, not the artifacts.

## Check it

Start the system for the first time:

```bash
cd system-host
dotnet run
```

Leave it running and, from the workspace root in a second terminal, inspect what was staged for the extractor:

```bash
ls system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/
```

```
inbound.yaml  poll.yaml  pubsub.yaml
```

```bash
grep "type:" system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml
```

```
  type: pubsub.redis
```

The two local components passed through; the pub/sub is now the system's — generated, not written. Stop the host with Ctrl+C — the next chapter runs it for real.

!!! check "Recap"
    - Component resolution is decided by whoever starts the sidecar: the local directory standalone, the staged overlay under the SystemHost
    - Local components pass through untouched; a generated component with the same `metadata.name` replaces its local counterpart
    - The system's components are generated from chapter 3's declaration; the staged set under `obj/` is inspectable, but regenerated on every start
    - Code and component names are identical in both modes; only the backing changes

# Gap analysis: system tutorial vs CLI / templates / intropy-topology

## Context

The system tutorial (`intropy-techdocs/docs/tutorials/system/`, served at http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/) walks through composing two integrations (`order-extractor`, `order-loader`) into an `order-flow` system via a SystemHost. The task: verify every claim the tutorial makes against the actual implementations — the Go CLI (`tooling/intropy-cli`, branch `feature/system`), the templates (`blueprints` repo), and the .NET topology library (`intropy-topology`) — and recommend, per gap, whether the fix belongs in the tutorial or the implementation.

## Tutorial claims inventory (baseline)

### CLI
- `int create <template> -n <Name> -s key=value -s topic=orders -o <dir>`
- Dependency rendering: first render creates `Contracts/` from `shared-contracts` ("created dependency Contracts from template shared-contracts"); second detects and skips ("dependency Contracts already scaffolded from shared-contracts — skipped")
- `.intropy/scaffold.json` records blueprint kind + topic param
- `sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host` reads scaffold records, generates: `OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj`, `Program.cs` (two-backend dispatch), `OrderFlowSystem.cs`, `Topics.cs` (TopicRef<Order> typed with contract type), `Properties/launchSettings.json`, `Taskfile.yml`; no dapr-components dir
- Contracts record marked as shared library → ProjectReference, never a component
- Name derivation OrderFlow → order-flow

### Templates
- `extractor`: params organization, topic; sample logic sweep→transform In→Order→publish→delete, long-running; layout with poll/inbound/pubsub components + sample-data; log lines "Swept 1 file from inbound", "Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)"
- `loader`: pubsub + destination components; subscribe→deserialize→validate→map Out→write {orderId}.json; log "Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)"; output {"OrderId","CustomerId","LoadedAt","Status"}
- `shared-contracts`: Contracts.csproj, Order.cs, OrderLine.cs; referenced ../../Contracts/Contracts.csproj
- `task run` seeds sample and starts Dapr with --resources-path ./local/dapr-components
- Integrations bind topic/component names from runtime config (host-injectable)

### intropy-topology
- API: ISystemDefinition{SystemName, Define(SystemBuilder)}, AddExtractor/AddLoader, Publishes/Subscribes (kind-constrained at compile time), TopicRef<T>.Define(pubsub, topic)
- IntropyAspire.RunAsync / IntropyGenerate.RunAsync; verbs check|graph|generate
- check output "ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components)."; errors ITP208/ITP209 with exact wording
- graph JSON: {systemName, components[{name,kind,publishes/subscribes}], topics[{pubsub,name,contract}]}
- Run backend: generates Redis pubsub components (localhost:6379), staged overlay under obj/dapr-components/<integration>/ keyed on metadata.name, --resources-path to staged dir
- Redis container auto-provisioned; subscribers start before publishers; OTLP injected (no Grafana under host)
- Caveat box in ch3 already hedges: runtime config binding "still landing in the tooling"

## Findings

(to be filled from exploration agents)

## Recommendations

# Gap analysis: system tutorial vs CLI / templates / intropy-topology

## Context

The system tutorial (`intropy-techdocs/docs/tutorials/system/`, served at http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/) walks through composing two integrations (`order-extractor`, `order-loader`) into an `order-flow` system via a SystemHost. The task: verify every claim the tutorial makes against the actual implementations — the Go CLI (`tooling/intropy-cli`, branch `feature/system`), the templates (`blueprints` repo), and the .NET topology library (`intropy-topology`) — and recommend, per gap, whether the fix belongs in the tutorial or the implementation.

## Tutorial claims inventory (baseline)

### CLI
- `int create <template> -n <Name> -s key=value -s topic=orders -o <dir>`
- Dependency rendering: first render creates `Contracts/` from `shared-contracts` ("created dependency Contracts from template shared-contracts"); second detects and skips ("dependency Contracts already scaffolded from shared-contracts — skipped")
- `.intropy/scaffold.json` records blueprint kind + topic param
- `sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host` reads scaffold records, generates: `OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj`, `Program.cs` (two-backend dispatch), `OrderFlowSystem.cs`, `Topics.cs` (TopicRef<Order> typed with contract type), `Properties/launchSettings.json`, `Taskfile.yml`; no dapr-components dir
- Contracts record marked as shared library → ProjectReference, never a component
- Name derivation OrderFlow → order-flow

### Templates
- `extractor`: params organization, topic; sample logic sweep→transform In→Order→publish→delete, long-running; layout with poll/inbound/pubsub components + sample-data; log lines "Swept 1 file from inbound", "Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)"
- `loader`: pubsub + destination components; subscribe→deserialize→validate→map Out→write {orderId}.json; log "Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)"; output {"OrderId","CustomerId","LoadedAt","Status"}
- `shared-contracts`: Contracts.csproj, Order.cs, OrderLine.cs; referenced ../../Contracts/Contracts.csproj
- `task run` seeds sample and starts Dapr with --resources-path ./local/dapr-components
- Integrations bind topic/component names from runtime config (host-injectable)

### intropy-topology
- API: ISystemDefinition{SystemName, Define(SystemBuilder)}, AddExtractor/AddLoader, Publishes/Subscribes (kind-constrained at compile time), TopicRef<T>.Define(pubsub, topic)
- IntropyAspire.RunAsync / IntropyGenerate.RunAsync; verbs check|graph|generate
- check output "ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components)."; errors ITP208/ITP209 with exact wording
- graph JSON: {systemName, components[{name,kind,publishes/subscribes}], topics[{pubsub,name,contract}]}
- Run backend: generates Redis pubsub components (localhost:6379), staged overlay under obj/dapr-components/<integration>/ keyed on metadata.name, --resources-path to staged dir
- Redis container auto-provisioned; subscribers start before publishers; OTLP injected (no Grafana under host)
- Caveat box in ch3 already hedges: runtime config binding "still landing in the tooling"

Both are `./local/storage/{{ .connector }}`:

- `loader/skeleton/local/dapr-components/destination.yaml.tmpl`: identical shape → `./local/storage/order-loader-destination`

`extractor/skeleton/src/Configuration/Constants.cs.tmpl` and the loader's equivalent are **compile-time `const string`s** baked at scaffold time:

Written by `internal/template/create.go:115-127` via `WriteScaffold` (`internal/template/scaffold.go:104`) to `<projectRoot>/.intropy/scaffold.json`. Schema (`scaffold.go:58-89`): `schemaVersion`, `template`, `owner`, `repo`, `version`, `values`, `role`, `blockKind`, `dataFlow`, `dependsOn[]{template,dir}`.

For `extractor` with `name=OrderExtractor organization=Fluxia topic=orders contract=Order` it records:
- `blockKind: "extractor"`, `dataFlow: "in"` (from labels `intropy.dev/block-kind`, `intropy.dev/data-flow`); loader → `"loader"` / `"out"`
- `values`: all parameters **plus** the derived `spec.values` (`values.go:62` `renderDerivedValues`) — `topic: "orders"`, `contract: "Order"`, `organization: "Fluxia"`, `empty: false`, `appId: "order-extractor"`, `contracts: "Contracts"`, `pubsub: "pubsub"`, `connector: "order-extractor-source"`
- `dependsOn: [{ "template": "shared-contracts", "dir": "../Contracts" }]`
- no `role` for extractor/loader; the sibling `Contracts/.intropy/scaffold.json` gets `role: "shared-library"` and no `blockKind`

`sys create` consumes exactly this: `internal/system/assemble.go:47` skips records whose `blockKind` is neither `extractor` nor `loader`; `assemble.go:110` errors if no `RoleSharedLibrary` project is found because `Topics.cs` needs the contract type.

---

## Additional things the templates render that the tutorial's trees omit

1. **Platform-service dependencies are mandatory, not optional.** Both pipelines call `.WithIdempotency(...)` and `.WithBusinessIncidents(...)`, and `Program.cs` registers `AddIdempotencyServiceClient()` / `AddBusinessIncidentServiceClient()`. `task run` therefore needs Docker up (`local/platform-services/compose.yaml` + 5 component yamls + two `HTTPEndpoint` components on `127.0.0.1:8080` / `:8081`).
2. **Idempotency behavior visible in the happy path**: re-seeding/re-publishing the same order **cancels** instead of duplicating, logging `Cancelled ORD-1001 as a duplicate (idempotency check)`.
3. **CloudEvent envelope constants** — `EventSource = urn:Fluxia:order-extractor`, `EventType = fluxia.orders.extracted`.
4. **`Dockerfile` requires a named build context**: `docker build --build-context contracts=../Contracts -t order-extractor .` (chiseled .NET 10 runtime).
5. **`AGENTS.md` + `CLAUDE.md`** are rendered in every template (`CLAUDE.md` is just `@AGENTS.md`) and document the component to coding agents.
6. **`empty: true` mode** — all step bodies become `NotImplementedException`, `sample-order.json` renders blank, `OrderLine.cs` renders blank, `Order`/`In`/`Out` become empty records.
7. **`--version` matters** — extractor/loader/shared-contracts do not exist on `main`; the examples' documented `--version main` is wrong for these templates.
8. **`system-host` template + `intropy sys create`** exist and generate `Topics.cs` / `Connectors.cs` / `<Name>System.cs` from the scaffold records; `.intropy/scaffold.json`'s `contract` and `connector` values are exactly what that codegen reads.
9. Test frameworks pinned: xUnit 2.9.3 + NSubstitute 5.3.0, `net10.0`; app packages `Intropy.Framework.Blocks` 0.2.3, `Intropy.Framework.Adapters` 0.2.3, `Dapr.Client` 1.17.9 (loader adds `Dapr.Messaging` 1.17.9).</result>

If the placeholder file is absent, codegen refuses rather than adding a second `ISystemDefinition` (`codegen.go:105-109`; test `create_test.go:463-475`).

### 6. Generated `Program.cs` — **SUPPORTED**

It is not generated by the CLI at all; it's copied verbatim from `intropy-templates/system-host/skeleton/Program.cs` (static file, no `.tmpl`). Actual content (lines 1-18): `using System.Reflection;` + `using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;` + `using Intropy.Topology.Generation;`, a comment block documenting `run`/`check`/`graph`/`generate ./out`, then:

```csharp
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();

return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);
```

Exactly as claimed (the tutorial just omits `using System.Reflection;`).

### 7. `Topics.cs` typing / pubsub + topic resolution — **SUPPORTED**

Template: `internal/system/codegen.go:16-29`. Emitted file starts `using Intropy.Topology;` + `using {{ .Shared.Name }};` (i.e. `using Contracts;`), then per topic:

```csharp
public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
```

Resolution, all from scaffold records in `internal/system/assemble.go`:
- **contract type** ← `values.contract` of each extractor/loader record (`assemble.go:60-63`). Missing → hard error with re-scaffold guidance, raised **before any network I/O** (`create.go:101-118` runs before `template.Create`; test `create_test.go:438-461`).
- **pubsub component** ← `values.pubsub`, with a CLI-side fallback to the literal `"pubsub"` for older records (`assemble.go:64-67`, `stringValueDefault` `:174-179`). Templates set it via `spec.values.pubsub: 'pubsub'` (`extractor/template.yaml:61`, `loader:61`, `system-host:35`).
- **topic name** ← `values.topic` (`assemble.go:56-59`); C# field = `pascalIdent(topic)` → `orders` → `Orders` (`assemble.go:98,184-194`).
- **contract namespace** ← the shared-library record's `values.name` (`assemble.go:34-40`, `model.go:39-42`).
- Topics are keyed by `(pubsub, topic)`, deduped, sorted, and conflicting contracts on the same key are an error (`assemble.go:92-100`, `:119-136`).

Expected output is pinned by test `internal/system/create_test.go:173-182`.

### 8. blockKind → builder method, topic → Publishes/Subscribes — **SUPPORTED**

`internal/system/codegen.go:120-135`: `Kind == template.BlockKindExtractor` → `AddExtractor` + `Publishes` (+ `.From(Connectors.X)`); anything else reaching that point → `AddLoader` + `Subscribes` (+ `.To(Connectors.X)`). Only those two kinds survive `Assemble` (`assemble.go:47-49`). Emission line: `codegen.go:55`

```
builder.{{ .Add }}("{{ .AppID }}"){{ .From }}.{{ .Edge }}(Topics.{{ .Field }}){{ .To }};
```

Component id is `values.appId` (`assemble.go:52-55`), derived by the templates as `{{ .name | kebabcase | replace "." "-" }}` (`extractor/template.yaml:52`). Duplicate appIds are an error (`assemble.go:80-83`). Real output for the tutorial workspace (`create_test.go:184-197`):

```csharp
builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").From(Connectors.OrderExtractorSource).Publishes(Topics.Orders);
builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders).To(Connectors.OrderLoaderDestination);
```

The tutorial's version (no `.From`/`.To`) is exactly the **legacy** shape produced only when the template release has no `Connectors.cs` placeholder (`create_test.go:214-227`) — see claim 10.

### 9. Contracts as shared library, never a component — **SUPPORTED**

- Marked by manifest label `intropy.dev/template-role: shared-library` (`intropy-templates/shared-contracts/template.yaml:11-13`), copied into the record's `role` field (`internal/template/scaffold.go:19-29,91-93`, `create.go:123`, `dependencies.go:139`).
- `Assemble` branches on `e.Role == template.RoleSharedLibrary` first and `continue`s, so it never becomes a component (`internal/system/assemble.go:34-40`); exactly one is required (`:108-117`).
- Referenced from the host by textual insertion before `</Project>` with `IsAspireProjectResource="false"` so Aspire doesn't orchestrate the class library (`internal/system/csproj.go:16-39`, path computed relatively at `:43-57`, called from `create.go:114-118,172-175`). Template leaves a comment at the insertion point (`system-host/skeleton/{{ .projectName }}.SystemHost.csproj.tmpl:23-25`). Asserted: `create_test.go:276-285` → `<ProjectReference Include="../Contracts/Contracts.csproj" IsAspireProjectResource="false" />`.
- The existing system host itself is also excluded on re-runs via `role: system-host` (`assemble.go:41-43`; warning `skipping <dir>: an existing system host`, test `create_test.go:419-436`).

### 10. Connectors (`From`/`To`, `Transport.File`, `test/<connector>/`) — **SUPPORTED; the tutorial under-reports this**

- Connector name comes from the component record's `values.connector`, derived by the templates as `<appId>-source` (extractor, `extractor/template.yaml:63-67`) and `<appId>-destination` (loader, `loader/template.yaml:62-67`). No CLI-side default — a record without it keeps its component but gets no `From`/`To`, with a warning (`assemble.go:70-78`; test `create_test.go:341-383`).
- `Connectors.cs` template: `codegen.go:31-43` → `ConnectorRef.Define("order-extractor-source", Transport.File("./test/order-extractor-source"));` (expected output `create_test.go:199-210`).
- Drop folders `<<<host>>>/test/<connector>/` are created so an extractor's first poll doesn't miss the directory (`create.go:163-171`).
- Graceful degradation: if the rendered template has no `Connectors.cs` placeholder (release predates connectors), the file is **not** created, a warning is printed, and the system class is emitted without `From`/`To` (`codegen.go:90-97`, `create.go:156-162`; test `create_test.go:310-339`). This is why the tutorial's snippet in claim 8 looks the way it does.
- Validation extras: duplicate connector names error out (`assemble.go:85-90`), and two connectors that collapse to the same C# identifier error out (`assemble.go:143-149`), same for topic fields (`:130-136`).
- Other things the tutorial doesn't mention that `sys create` produces: the host's own `.intropy/scaffold.json`, the `--output-json` `CreateResult` document containing the full assembled `Summary` (name/components/topics/connectors/sharedLibrary — `create.go:49-67,183-221`), and the stderr summary line (`create.go:177-178`): `assembled system "order-flow": 2 component(s), 1 topic(s), 2 connector(s), contracts from Contracts`.

### 11. `-n OrderFlow` → `order-flow` — **SUPPORTED**

`internal/system/create.go:96` uses `xstrings.ToKebabCase(opts.Name)` explicitly for sprig parity with the templates' `{{ .name | kebabcase }}`, so `OrderFlow` and `order-flow` are equivalent inputs. The kebab name becomes `SystemName`, the default output dir (`:97-99`), and the only value passed to the template (`:123`). Tests: `create_test.go:385-398` (output defaults to `./order-flow`), `:189` (`public string SystemName => "order-flow";`), `:299`. Template's `name` pattern is DNS-1123 (`system-host/template.yaml:28`), which the pre-kebabing satisfies.

---

## TODO / unimplemented / rough edges in the `sys create` flow

No `TODO`/`FIXME`/`not implemented` markers exist anywhere in the CLI's non-test Go source (grep over `cmd/` + `internal/` came back empty). The `TODO(intropy)` strings live only in the *template placeholders* (`system-host/skeleton/Topics.cs.tmpl:8`, `Connectors.cs.tmpl:13`, `{{ .systemClass }}.cs.tmpl:15`) and are overwritten by codegen. Functional limits worth flagging in a tutorial:

1. **Only `extractor` and `loader` assemble.** Any other `blockKind` (e.g. `reconciler`) is skipped with a warning (`assemble.go:47-49`; test `assemble_test.go:316-322`); so are records with no `blockKind` at all.
2. **Exactly one shared-library** is required; zero or 2+ is a hard error (`assemble.go:108-117`).
3. **Codegen overwrites unconditionally.** `Topics.cs`, `Connectors.cs` and `<Name>System.cs` are rewritten from the records with no merge/preserve of hand edits (`codegen.go:145-154`), even though the template comments invite you to edit them afterwards. Re-running `sys create` needs `--force` (`create.go:126` → `ensureOutputDir`, `internal/template/create.go:212-230`) and will discard manual topology changes.
4. **Scan root isn't a flag** — always cwd (`create.go:69-72`); `StartDir` is test-only in practice.
5. **`sys` has only `create`** — no `list`/`graph`/`run`/`add` verbs; inspection is delegated to the generated host (`dotnet run -- check|graph|generate`, `Taskfile.yml.tmpl`).
6. **`int` help overstates scope**: `int.go:8` says "create new ones and run existing ones", but there is no `int run`.
7. **Release-channel mismatch (biggest tutorial blocker)**: `extractor`, `loader`, `shared-contracts`, `system-host` only exist in *pre-release* tags of `intropy-templates`, while both `int create` and `sys create` default to GitHub's `releases/latest` = `v0.1.7`. Every tutorial command needs an explicit `--version v0.2.1-beta.6` until a stable release ships.</result>

# Gap analysis: system tutorial vs CLI / templates / intropy-topology

## Context

The system tutorial (`intropy-techdocs/docs/tutorials/system/`, served at http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/) walks through composing two integrations (`order-extractor`, `order-loader`) into an `order-flow` system via a SystemHost. The task: verify every claim the tutorial makes against the actual implementations — the Go CLI (`tooling/intropy-cli`, branch `feature/system`), the templates (`blueprints` repo), and the .NET topology library (`intropy-topology`) — and recommend, per gap, whether the fix belongs in the tutorial or the implementation.

## Tutorial claims inventory (baseline)

### CLI
- `int create <template> -n <Name> -s key=value -s topic=orders -o <dir>`
- Dependency rendering: first render creates `Contracts/` from `shared-contracts` ("created dependency Contracts from template shared-contracts"); second detects and skips ("dependency Contracts already scaffolded from shared-contracts — skipped")
- `.intropy/scaffold.json` records blueprint kind + topic param
- `sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host` reads scaffold records, generates: `OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj`, `Program.cs` (two-backend dispatch), `OrderFlowSystem.cs`, `Topics.cs` (TopicRef<Order> typed with contract type), `Properties/launchSettings.json`, `Taskfile.yml`; no dapr-components dir
- Contracts record marked as shared library → ProjectReference, never a component
- Name derivation OrderFlow → order-flow

### Templates
- `extractor`: params organization, topic; sample logic sweep→transform In→Order→publish→delete, long-running; layout with poll/inbound/pubsub components + sample-data; log lines "Swept 1 file from inbound", "Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)"
- `loader`: pubsub + destination components; subscribe→deserialize→validate→map Out→write {orderId}.json; log "Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)"; output {"OrderId","CustomerId","LoadedAt","Status"}
- `shared-contracts`: Contracts.csproj, Order.cs, OrderLine.cs; referenced ../../Contracts/Contracts.csproj
- `task run` seeds sample and starts Dapr with --resources-path ./local/dapr-components
- Integrations bind topic/component names from runtime config (host-injectable)

### intropy-topology
- API: ISystemDefinition{SystemName, Define(SystemBuilder)}, AddExtractor/AddLoader, Publishes/Subscribes (kind-constrained at compile time), TopicRef<T>.Define(pubsub, topic)
- IntropyAspire.RunAsync / IntropyGenerate.RunAsync; verbs check|graph|generate
- check output "ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components)."; errors ITP208/ITP209 with exact wording
- graph JSON: {systemName, components[{name,kind,publishes/subscribes}], topics[{pubsub,name,contract}]}
- Run backend: generates Redis pubsub components (localhost:6379), staged overlay under obj/dapr-components/<integration>/ keyed on metadata.name, --resources-path to staged dir
- Redis container auto-provisioned; subscribers start before publishers; OTLP injected (no Grafana under host)
- Caveat box in ch3 already hedges: runtime config binding "still landing in the tooling"

(to be filled: per-gap fix location — tutorial vs CLI vs templates vs topology lib)

Exactly as claimed (the tutorial just omits `using System.Reflection;`).

5. **`sys` has only `create`** — no `list`/`graph`/`run`/`add` verbs; inspection is delegated to the generated host (`dotnet run -- check|graph|generate`, `Taskfile.yml.tmpl`).
6. **`int` help overstates scope**: `int.go:8` says "create new ones and run existing ones", but there is no `int run`.
7. **Release-channel mismatch (biggest tutorial blocker)**: `extractor`, `loader`, `shared-contracts`, `system-host` only exist in *pre-release* tags of `intropy-templates`, while both `int create` and `sys create` default to GitHub's `releases/latest` = `v0.1.7`. # Gap analysis: system tutorial vs CLI / templates / intropy-topology

## Context

The system tutorial (`intropy-techdocs/docs/tutorials/system/`, served at http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/) walks through composing two integrations (`order-extractor`, `order-loader`) into an `order-flow` system via a SystemHost. The task: verify every claim the tutorial makes against the actual implementations — the Go CLI (`tooling/intropy-cli`, branch `feature/system`), the templates (`blueprints` repo), and the .NET topology library (`intropy-topology`) — and recommend, per gap, whether the fix belongs in the tutorial or the implementation.

## Tutorial claims inventory (baseline)

### CLI
- `int create <template> -n <Name> -s key=value -s topic=orders -o <dir>`
- Dependency rendering: first render creates `Contracts/` from `shared-contracts` ("created dependency Contracts from template shared-contracts"); second detects and skips ("dependency Contracts already scaffolded from shared-contracts — skipped")
- `.intropy/scaffold.json` records blueprint kind + topic param
- `sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host` reads scaffold records, generates: `OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj`, `Program.cs` (two-backend dispatch), `OrderFlowSystem.cs`, `Topics.cs` (TopicRef<Order> typed with contract type), `Properties/launchSettings.json`, `Taskfile.yml`; no dapr-components dir
- Contracts record marked as shared library → ProjectReference, never a component
- Name derivation OrderFlow → order-flow

### Templates
- `extractor`: params organization, topic; sample logic sweep→transform In→Order→publish→delete, long-running; layout with poll/inbound/pubsub components + sample-data; log lines "Swept 1 file from inbound", "Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)"
- `loader`: pubsub + destination components; subscribe→deserialize→validate→map Out→write {orderId}.json; log "Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)"; output {"OrderId","CustomerId","LoadedAt","Status"}
- `shared-contracts`: Contracts.csproj, Order.cs, OrderLine.cs; referenced ../../Contracts/Contracts.csproj
- `task run` seeds sample and starts Dapr with --resources-path ./local/dapr-components
- Integrations bind topic/component names from runtime config (host-injectable)

### intropy-topology
- API: ISystemDefinition{SystemName, Define(SystemBuilder)}, AddExtractor/AddLoader, Publishes/Subscribes (kind-constrained at compile time), TopicRef<T>.Define(pubsub, topic)
- IntropyAspire.RunAsync / IntropyGenerate.RunAsync; verbs check|graph|generate
- check output "ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components)."; errors ITP208/ITP209 with exact wording
- graph JSON: {systemName, components[{name,kind,publishes/subscribes}], topics[{pubsub,name,contract}]}
- Run backend: generates Redis pubsub components (localhost:6379), staged overlay under obj/dapr-components/<integration>/ keyed on metadata.name, --resources-path to staged dir
- Redis container auto-provisioned; subscribers start before publishers; OTLP injected (no Grafana under host)
- Caveat box in ch3 already hedges: runtime config binding "still landing in the tooling"

## Findings

### Templates (authoritative: `tooling/intropy-templates`, branch `feature/more-templates`)

Templates: extractor, loader, shared-contracts, system-host, hello-world, transactional. NOT on `main` — extractor/loader/shared-contracts only exist on `feature/more-templates`. `blueprints/` clone is stale (only hello-world + transactional). CLI fetches templates from GitHub at runtime (no embed).

**Gaps found:**
1. **`contract` is a required param** the tutorial's commands omit (`-s contract=Order` missing) — render prompts or fails with --no-input. Template READMEs also omit it (stale).
2. **No cron binding / poll.yaml** — polling is in-process `PeriodicTimer` (`Constants.PollIntervalSeconds = 5`), not a Dapr cron binding. Tutorial's tree shows `poll.yaml` which doesn't exist.
3. **Connector component naming**: inbound/destination components are named `binding.{{ .connector }}` (e.g. `binding.order-extractor-source`), not `inbound`/`destination`. Files are inbound.yaml/destination.yaml but metadata.name differs.
4. **Storage paths**: `local/storage/<connector>/` (e.g. `order-extractor-source`, `order-loader-destination`), not `local/storage/inbound/` / `local/storage/destination/`. Tutorial paths match the older `transactional` template — likely copied stale.
5. **Log line**: actual is `Swept {Count} file(s) from inbound` → "Swept 1 file(s) from inbound", not "Swept 1 file from inbound". Other logs match ("Published ... to topic orders (pubsub)", "Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)").
6. **Runtime config claim contradicted**: topic/pubsub/binding names are compile-time consts baked at scaffold (`Constants.cs.tmpl`); no IConfiguration/env binding. The real seam is the Dapr component *name* (`binding.<connector>`, `pubsub`) that the host overlay replaces — ch3 "How the declaration reaches the code" section is wrong about mechanism.
7. **Loader `task run` doesn't seed**; extractor seeds into `local/storage/<connector>/`. Loader Taskfile ships a `publish` task (ORD-2001 data) the tutorial types by hand.
8. **`task run` requires Docker** even standalone: `services:up` starts lgtm + Idempotency + Business Incident platform services; pipelines mandatorily call WithIdempotency/WithBusinessIncidents. Tutorial says docker-compose is "local observability stack — standalone runs only" and doesn't mention platform services as prerequisites of `task run`.
9. Tutorial trees omit rendered files: Dockerfile, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, idempotency/business-incident HTTPEndpoint yamls, local/platform-services/, src/Configuration/Constants.cs, appsettings.json etc. (Acceptable simplification, but poll.yaml is invented.)
10. sample-order.json has **two** lines (tutorial's dapr publish example with one line is its own data, fine); shape matches, ORD-1001/CUST-42 correct.
11. scaffold.json schema confirmed: schemaVersion, template, owner, repo, version, values (params + derived appId/contracts/pubsub/connector), role, blockKind, dataFlow, dependsOn[{template,dir}]. Contracts gets `role: "shared-library"`. Matches tutorial's story.
12. ProjectReference `../../Contracts/Contracts.csproj` ✅ (from src/ one level down). Tutorial tree shows csproj implicitly — fine.
13. Idempotency duplicate-cancel behavior surfaces in happy path (re-seeding same order logs "Cancelled ... as a duplicate") — tutorial never warns.

# Gap analysis: system tutorial vs CLI / templates / Intropy.Topology

## Context

The system tutorial (`intropy-techdocs/docs/tutorials/system/`, 6 pages) walks through composing `order-extractor` + `order-loader` into an `order-flow` system via a SystemHost. Every claim was verified against the three implementations:

- **CLI**: `tooling/intropy-cli` (branch `feature/system`)
- **Templates**: `tooling/intropy-templates` (branch `feature/more-templates`, the authoritative checkout — `~/dev/intropy/blueprints` is a stale second clone)
- **Topology library**: `tooling/Intropy.Topology` (branch `feature/minimal-core` — NOT `~/dev/intropy/intropy-topology`, which is a stale single-commit fork with a different API)

Overall: the CLI matches the tutorial best (messages verbatim, scaffold.json schema, sys create flow all confirmed). The biggest divergences are (a) two hard blockers that make the tutorial un-runnable today, (b) the tutorial under-reports connectors, which `sys create` and the library fully implement, and (c) chapter 3's "runtime config" mechanism describes unshipped design.

## Blockers (tutorial cannot be completed today)

### B1. Template release channel — fix in **intropy-templates (release process)**

builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").From(Connectors.OrderExtractorSource).Publishes(Topics.Orders);

- Storage paths are `local/storage/<connector>/` (`order-extractor-source`, `order-loader-destination`), not `local/storage/inbound|destination/` — the tutorial's paths match the older `transactional` template (stale copy).

**Fix**: remove it from the tree; one clause noting the extractor polls in-process every 5 s.

Actual line format is `  ITP208 [Error] orders: The topic 'orders' on pubsub 'pubsub' is published but no component subscribes to it.` (target = bare topic name, sentence-cased message; tested + documented in `docs/concepts/validation.md`). Tutorial shows an invented `topic 'orders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is published but...` format.
**Fix**: paste real output. (If the tutorial's format is considered better, that's a library change — not recommended; the current format is snapshot-tested.)

### C6. Log line wording — fix in **tutorial** (or micro-fix in templates)
Actual: `Swept 1 file(s) from inbound` (template literal `{Count} file(s)`). Tutorial: `Swept 1 file from inbound`.
**Fix**: match tutorial to reality; optionally nicer pluralization in the template later.

### C7. `task run` prerequisites and behavior — fix in **tutorial**, decision needed in **templates**
- `task run` (both templates) depends on `services:up` = `docker compose up -d --wait` for lgtm **plus Idempotency and Business Incident platform services**; the pipelines call `.WithIdempotency()`/`.WithBusinessIncidents()` unconditionally via `HTTPEndpoint` components on 127.0.0.1:8080/8081. | Fix | Where |
|---|---|

| Stale READMEs on `feature/minimal-core` still describe Microcks/`IDevProfile`/old `Generate` signature (cut by ADR 0009) | Intropy.Topology docs |

2. **Tutorial edits** (`intropy-techdocs/docs/tutorials/system/*.md`): B3, C1–C6, C8, omissions — one PR.

The tutorial's snippet (no `From`/`To`) is the legacy degraded output for releases lacking a `Connectors.cs` placeholder. Tutorial: "each integration binds its topic and component names from runtime configuration... the host generates it from this declaration and injects it." **Fix**: rewrite that ch3 section to say the seam is the Dapr component *name* (names baked at scaffold, backing swapped by the overlay), and drop/repurpose the caveat box. - `task run` (both templates) depends on `services:up` = `docker compose up -d --wait` for lgtm **plus Idempotency and Business Incident platform services**; the pipelines call `.WithIdempotency()`/`.WithBusinessIncidents()` unconditionally via `HTTPEndpoint` components on 127.0.0.1:8080/8081. Tutorial calls docker-compose an "observability stack — standalone runs only".

So ch5 likely requires the platform-services compose stack to be running too — and re-dropping `ORD-1001` (already published in ch1) may be **cancelled as an idempotent duplicate**, breaking the ch5 payoff.

**Fix**: (tutorial) document the platform-services prerequisite in ch1/ch5, mention `task publish` in ch2, and use a fresh order id in ch5 (or explain the duplicate-cancel log line). - Startup ordering is real (publishers `WaitFor` subscribers) but waits on the subscriber resource being *Running*, not its subscription being *registered*; cycles disable ordering with only a stderr warning. Ch5's "registered its subscription before the extractor began polling" overpromises.
**Fix**: soften both sentences.
